title: Seville Orange Marmalade
subtitle: The classic bitter orange preserve
excerpt: Bitter Seville oranges and lemons shredded and simmered with sugar to a glossy, deeply flavoured marmalade. A six-week season in January to make a year's supply. Spread on hot buttered toast, nothing comes close.

recipe.sourceNotes: Marmalade in Britain specifically denotes a citrus preserve made from the whole fruit including the peel; the word derives from the Portuguese marmelada, a quince paste that arrived in Britain in the sixteenth century, though the modern citrus marmalade is a British development. Seville oranges were established as the definitive marmalade orange by the early eighteenth century, when James Keiller of Dundee began producing marmalade commercially from bitter Spanish oranges. Seville oranges are in season for only six weeks in January and February; their high pectin and acid content makes them ideal for marmalade without added pectin. The coarse-cut variety, with long peel shreds, is the most distinctive British style.

recipeTools.notes: A very large preserving pan or stockpot of at least 8 litres capacity.

content.text: The pips and pith contain most of the pectin: tie them in a muslin bag and simmer them in the pot with the fruit to extract their setting power. Test for set with a cold plate: drop a small spoonful onto a plate kept in the freezer; if it wrinkles when pushed with a finger, the marmalade will set. A temperature of 105 C on a sugar thermometer is the reliable indicator.

Halve the oranges and squeeze out the juice, collecting the pips. Cut the squeezed halves into quarters and slice the peel finely or coarsely according to preference. Put the pips and any excess pith into a piece of muslin and tie into a bag. Place the peel, juice, muslin bag, and 2 litres of cold water in a large pan. Bring to the boil and simmer for 1.5 to 2 hours until the peel is completely tender.

Remove the muslin bag and squeeze it well into the pan to extract all the pectin. Add the sugar and lemon juice. Stir over low heat until every grain of sugar has dissolved; do not boil until fully dissolved or the marmalade may not set. Then bring to a rolling boil and boil hard for 10 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Test for set: place a teaspoon of marmalade on a cold plate from the freezer. Leave for 1 minute, then push with a finger. If the surface wrinkles and the marmalade does not flood back, setting point has been reached. Remove from the heat and skim any foam from the surface. Leave to stand for 20 minutes before potting into sterilised jars. Seal immediately.
